claims.claim: REMOVED and REPLACED, the sweep worst finding (F-UNSOURCED): "In the 118th Congress (2023-2024), roughly 19,000 measures were introduced in the House and Senate combined. 274 became law - about 1.4%." Uncited, and the sweep found real reporting on this exact 118th-Congress metric varying two- to threefold by counting method. The page now uses figures derived from the Congress.gov API for the 119th Congress and stored as data/ref-text/record-congress-119-measure-counts.txt: 18,500 measures introduced and 104 laws (102 public, 2 private) as of 2026-09-01. The percentage is GONE rather than recomputed - it mixed denominators, since simple and concurrent resolutions cannot become law - and the page states that the Congress is still in session so the figures are counts as of a date, not final totals. The stored record also carries an arithmetic check: the eight per-type counts sum to the all-measures total.

REMOVED, U-FLAG (sweep, its most-quoted line): "The chair decides. Not the majority of the committee - the chair," and "A committee member who disagrees can't force action." House Rule XI clause 2(c) contradicts this directly: three or more members may file a written request for a special meeting, and if the chair does not call it within three calendar days a MAJORITY of the committee may notice the meeting themselves and hold it. House Rule XIII clause 2(b)(2) likewise lets a majority force the filing of a report within seven calendar days. Both are now on the page with receipts. What survives, correctly narrowed, is that nothing in the rules obliges a committee to take up a measure referred to it.

REMOVED, F-UNSOURCED (sweep): the January 6th Select Committee example and the claim that select committees "can hold hearings and issue subpoenas but typically cannot report legislation to the full chamber." CRS 98-241 says the opposite of the second half - select committees are established "sometimes to conduct investigations and studies and, on other occasions, ALSO TO CONSIDER MEASURES." The section is now built from CRS description, including the example CRS itself gives (the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, which "operates, in many ways, like a permanent standing committee").

REMOVED, U-FLAG (sweep): "Conference committees have become less common; amendment ping-pong between the chambers has largely replaced them as the reconciliation mechanism for most legislation." A trend claim resting on nothing stored. The section now gives only CRS definition of what a conference committee is and does.

REMOVED, U-FLAG (sweep): "The committee chair's office receives hundreds or thousands of referrals per Congress and schedules hearings for a small fraction of them," and "Bills without a powerful sponsor, significant outside advocacy, or majority leadership support typically don't move." Unsourced volume and causal claims. Replaced with the referral rule itself (House Rule XII clause 2) and the Senate Rule XIV bypass.

REMOVED, unsourced: the descriptions of who testifies at hearings, that witnesses "submit written testimony in advance and give an oral summary", that transcripts are "available through the committee's website and through GovInfo" and are "often the most substantive source of technical analysis about what a bill does", and that markup "is usually public and streamed by the committee." None of it came from a stored source. The section now rests on House Rule XI clause 2(g)(1), which is what actually makes committee business public and which expressly covers the markup of legislation.

REMOVED, editorial plus unsourced: "Committee reports are significant documents. Courts and agency administrators sometimes consult them when interpreting ambiguous statutory language, on the theory that the report reflects the legislative intent of the enacting Congress." The word "significant" is banned by SYSTEM_PROMPT RULE 7 and the judicial-use claim rests on nothing stored. The section now states what Rule XIII clauses 2(b), 2(c), 3(b) and 3(c) actually require a report to contain.

REMOVED, U-FLAG (sweep): "The committee system creates multiple veto points" and the list of what bills that advance "tend to have" (bipartisan support, mandatory vehicles, crisis-driven urgency, leadership backing). Unsourced generalisations about legislative success. The section now makes the narrower point the rules support - the duties bind only after a committee has approved a measure - and points to the discharge rule as the route the rules do supply.

REMOVED, unsourced: the five paired House/Senate committee bullets and their jurisdiction summaries. Senate Rule XXV is not stored, so no Senate committee jurisdiction could be receipted. The list is now four HOUSE committees with their jurisdictions quoted from House Rule X, and the Senate appears only where CRS or a stored CRS report speaks to it.

CORRECTED and sourced: "The House currently has 20 standing committees; the Senate has 16" was flagged S-RISK by the sweep for having no as-of date. The counts are unchanged - CRS 98-241, updated November 25, 2025, gives exactly those figures for the 119th Congress - but the page now states the vintage, and adds the subcommittee, select, special and joint counts from the same source.

REWRITTEN: the closing site-description section previously asserted that "Passed House" or "Passed Senate" means a bill "cleared the relevant committee and floor," which is not what the labels encode. It now states only the label vocabulary, receipted against the stored corpus snapshot, and that each bill page links its Congress.gov record. No countable claim about the site is made, and data/ref-text/record-lp-site-facts.txt was NOT regenerated (batch instruction).

ROUND 2 FIX (carried from the congressional-oversight hostile pass, which found the identical defect on that page; re-derived here against hman-119-rule-xi.txt and CONFIRMED): the hearings-and-markup section rested entirely on clause 2(g)(1), which governs MEETINGS FOR THE TRANSACTION OF BUSINESS. Hearings are governed by clause 2(g)(2)(A) and carry a SHORTER closure list - national security, sensitive law enforcement information, or violating a law or rule of the House - with no defamation ground. The page presented the business-meeting list as covering hearings. Both provisions are now quoted and the difference stated. Both provisions also except "the Committee on Ethics or its subcommittees", which the draft had dropped from the quoted span; restored.

SOURCING NOTE: CRS 98-241 cites Senate Rule XXV for the Senate standing committees, but the Senate Manual is not among this ledger sources and Senate Rule XXV text was not fetched. Every Senate claim on the page is therefore attributed to CRS or to CRS RS22299, never presented as Senate rule text.

ROUND 2 FIX (hostile Sonnet pass 1, BLOCKING x2, adjudicated against record-crs-98-241-committee-types.txt and CONFIRMED): the House and Senate committee-count sentences were each quoted as ONE continuous run, but the stored CRS capture carries inline footnote markers inside both - "104 subcommittees 1 and two select committees" and "70 subcommittees 3 as well as". The quotation marks therefore promised verbatim text that silently closed two gaps. Both sentences are now quoted as separate verbatim fragments with the footnote convention stated on the page, and each fragment has its own ledger row. The per-fact ledger rows were already clean; the defect was introduced only when they were merged into single quotations in the prose.

ROUND 2 FIX (hostile Sonnet pass 1, BLOCKING, adjudicated and CONFIRMED): the lede asserted "Almost every measure Congress considers stops at a committee, and most stop there permanently." No registered source supports an attrition rate, and the article's OWN corpus snapshot points the other way for the bills this site tracks - 206 of 219 have advanced past committee, only 5 sit In Committee. This was the same substantive claim the ledger had already recorded as removed (the 19,000/274 statistic), surviving in prose form at the top of the page. Replaced with what the rules do establish: a committee is under no obligation to act on what it receives.

ROUND 2 FIX (hostile Sonnet pass 1, NON-BLOCKING): setting 18,500 measures introduced beside 104 laws in one sentence still invited the reader to compute a completion rate, which was the flaw in the statistic this rewrite removed - the denominators do not match, because concurrent and simple resolutions cannot become law. The laws figure is out of the lede; what remains is the measure count, the 2,505 resolutions inside it that are structurally incapable of becoming law, and the fact that the Congress is still in session. No rate is stated or implied.

The section now states only the label vocabulary, which the corpus snapshot does evidence, and says the action history lives on the Congress.gov record without characterising its completeness.

ROUND 2 FIX (hostile Sonnet pass 1, NON-BLOCKING): "The House Rules Committee's control of the floor schedule is the other side of the same problem" was an editorial framing tied to no source. Reworded to a structural statement.

ROUND 2 FIX (hostile Sonnet pass 1, NON-BLOCKING): the "still in session" qualifier traced through the measure-counts file to data/ref-text/record-congress-119-overview.txt, which was not in this ledger's sources[]. Registered, with its own claim row.

ROUND 2 FIX (hostile Sonnet pass 1, NOTE x2): three ledger rows carried clause labels that the page-break scrambles in hman-119-rule-xi.txt and hman-119-rule-xv.txt make unsafe to assert at sub-clause precision. No reader-facing text changes - the prose says "under the same clause", which is true either way.

BATCH-WIDE SWEEP (2026-09-02), the systemic defect of this batch: 104 instances across all seven articles where a comma, period, semicolon or colon sat INSIDE a closing quotation mark although the source has no such character at that point. American typographic convention puts them there; this site rule does not allow it, because a span in quotation marks is a promise of verbatimness and invented punctuation inside the marks breaks that promise for a reader checking the source. Two hostile passes had each flagged one or two instances individually, which produced iterative one-at-a-time fixes and, on one span, three successive wrong repairs. The class was instead resolved MECHANICALLY: a scanner extracted every quoted span on every page, tested it against the concatenated registered sources for that article, and where the span matched only after stripping one trailing punctuation character, moved that character outside the closing quote. Per-article counts: what-is-a-committee 32, discharge-petition 22, house-rules-committee 19, bill-numbering 12, congressional-oversight 8, how-to-read-a-bill 7, joint-resolution 4. A re-scan after the sweep returns zero. No word in any quotation changed; only the position of punctuation relative to the closing mark.

SWEEP FOLLOW-UP, adjudicated not fixed: after the punctuation sweep the scanner still flags a handful of spans per page. Every one was inspected. They fall into three groups, none a defect. (1) Nested-quote renderings, where the source own internal quotation marks arrive as HTML entities or as double-backtick/double-apostrophe pairs and the page renders them as single quotes so they can sit inside a double-quoted span - already adjudicated per-article in earlier rounds. (2) Scanner pairing artefacts, where an odd number of quote characters in a paragraph makes the scanner slice across a boundary and produce a span that was never on the page. (3) The literal string article-body, which is the class attribute the scanner picks up when it strips tags. Recorded so a future audit running the same scanner does not re-open them.

ROUND 2 FIX (hostile Sonnet pass 2, NON-BLOCKING, adjudicated against hman-119-rule-xiii.txt and CONFIRMED): the clause 3(b) record-vote requirement was quoted without the sentence immediately following it, which exempts votes taken in executive session by the Committee on Ethics. Same dropped-carve-out class as the two clause 2(g) Ethics exceptions already fixed on this page. Added.

ROUND 2 FIX (hostile Sonnet pass 2, NOTE): four ledger rows still certified figures the round-1 rewrite had removed from the lede - the 104/102/2 law counts and the September 1 as-of date, which left the page when the false-ratio framing was cut. A ledger row asserting a fact the prose no longer makes is exactly the orphan class the proseSha check exists to catch, and it would have carried into the published ledger as a receipt for text nobody could find. Rows dropped. The measure-count and session-status rows that DO correspond to surviving prose are untouched.

SWEEP CORRECTION (2026-09-02): the first quote-boundary sweep applied an outside-always rule, which was half right. The correct rule is two-sided - punctuation belongs INSIDE the closing quotation mark when the source sentence genuinely ends there, and OUTSIDE when the quote truncates mid-sentence. A second scanner was written to test both directions: for every quoted span it asks whether span+punctuation appears in the registered sources (then it belongs inside) or only span does (then outside). Across the seven articles it found 12 candidates for inside. Each was checked against the source bytes and only the genuine sentence-ends were moved: three on this batch (two on what-is-a-committee, one adjudicated the other way on house-rules-committee). The remaining nine were FALSE POSITIVES of the naive rule - semicolons and commas that are the page own list separators and merely happen to occur at the same point in the source. Those stay outside, because the punctuation is the article, not the quotation. The two already-published articles scanned clean in both directions.

MECHANICAL RETAG (2026-09-02): a hostile pass flagged three ledger rows typed "quote" whose prose actually paraphrases. Rather than fix three by hand, a detector compared every quote-typed row against the set of spans the page actually presents inside quotation marks. It found 84 such rows across the seven articles (house-rules-committee 21, how-to-read-a-bill 13, what-is-a-committee 12, congressional-oversight 10, discharge-petition 10, joint-resolution 9, bill-numbering 9) and retagged them "fact". The retag only weakens what the ledger claims about itself and never strengthens it; every receipt is unchanged and still verbatim. Same lesson as the punctuation class - a defect that recurs is cheaper to detect mechanically than to fix one instance at a time.
